scenario: AITA for not wanting to attend my great aunt's funeral? | So today I came home from college (Britain, so American High School, I think). The second I walk through the door my mum tells me that her grandma's sister has died. "Your great aunt Wyn died and the funeral will probably be soon." My first thoughts were 'Who?' and 'Why is she telling me this?' I have actually never heard this name before or met this person besides the one time I found out today I had met her when I was still extremely young and unable to walk for myself. This turned into a slight argument as, for some reason, she wanted me to go this funeral, despite knowing I am a really awkward person at funeral's for people I've met more than once, let along a funeral for someone I've met only once and have no idea who is part of the family. The argument ends with her trying to guilt-trip me by outright just saying "Fine, I'll go on my own." in a really sulky way. Her only arguments for me going were that I'd be going out of 'respect' and support for her, despite that she has never once mentioned this great aunt to me even though she supposedly played a massive hand in raising her as my grandmother, and that it's one of the few times we'll see the much larger branch of the family where it's likely to be a few hundred of us, about 10 of which I have seen more than once but still at most 10 times, maybe not even that. To me, it would feel like gatecrashing the funeral for someone else's family and that, even though I am part of the family, no one would want me there since I do not know nor did I know the person who died. I don't know how much this takes precedence over everything else but it felt like it had to reiterated a lot - I have never met this person besides the one time she met me when I was either 1 or 2 years old and the name has never been mentioned to me before now, at least not to my recollection. So, AITA for not wanting to attend someone who is practically a stranger to me's wedding for the sole reason that she's family?

Thanksgiving is next week and I'm responsible for preparing the turkey for the first time. My family has a specific recipe for it that everyone expects. How would you approach that?

Preparing your family’s Thanksgiving turkey for the first time can feel daunting, but with a structured approach, you can ensure success while staying true to tradition. Here’s a step-by-step guide to help you navigate the process with confidence: --- ### **1. Review the Recipe Thoroughly** - **Clarify details**: Ask a family member to confirm the exact recipe (e.g., brining method, seasoning, cooking time, temperature, and any special techniques like butter basting or herb stuffing). - **Check for notes**: Look for handwritten instructions, family traditions (e.g., "always add a splash of bourbon" or "let it rest for 30 minutes"), or adjustments (e.g., "reduce salt if using salted butter"). - **Gather tools**: Ensure you have all necessary equipment (meat thermometer, roasting pan, basting brush, etc.). --- ### **2. Plan Ahead (Critical for First-Timers!)** - **Buy the turkey early**: Fresh turkeys sell out quickly. Opt for a **whole turkey (12–14 lbs for 6–8 people)** or a **brined turkey (10–12 lbs)** if your recipe includes brining. Frozen turkeys require more thawing time (about 24 hours per 4–5 lbs in the fridge). - **Thawing**: If frozen, thaw in the fridge (not on the counter) starting **3–4 days before cooking**. Use the "day-by-day" thawing guide: - **Day 1**: Start thawing (e.g., a 12-lb turkey needs ~3 days). - **Day 2–3**: Continue thawing; check for ice buildup. - **Day before cooking**: Ensure it’s fully thawed (liquid should run clear). - **Prep workspace**: Clean and organize your kitchen, tools, and ingredients the day before. --- ### **3. Follow the Recipe Step-by-Step** Here’s a general framework based on common family recipes (adjust for specifics): #### **A. Brining (If Applicable)** - **Why**: Brining (soaking in saltwater) keeps the turkey juicy. If your recipe includes this, start **24–48 hours before cooking**. - **How**: - Dissolve **1 cup salt + ¼ cup sugar** per gallon of water (or use a pre-made brine). - Add **aromatics** (e.g., garlic, herbs, citrus peels) if the recipe specifies. - Submerge the turkey in a **large container** (use a weight to keep it submerged). - **Rinse before cooking** and pat dry. #### **B. Pre-Cooking Prep** - **Dry the turkey thoroughly**: Pat it dry with paper towels to ensure even browning. - **Seasoning**: - **Inside cavity**: Rub with butter, herbs (thyme, rosemary, sage), garlic, and salt/pepper as per the recipe. - **Outside**: Season generously with salt, pepper, and any other spices (e.g., sage, black peppercorn). - **Stuffing (if used)**: - Prepare stuffing **ahead** (day before) and refrigerate. - Stuff loosely into the cavity (overstuffing can dry it out). Some families prefer **separate stuffing** baked in a dish. #### **C. Roasting** - **Oven setup**: - Preheat oven to **325°F (165°C)**—lower temps ensure even cooking. - Place turkey **breast-side up** on a rack in a roasting pan (for airflow). - Add **liquid** (water, broth, or apple juice) to the pan to prevent drying. - **Basting**: - Baste every **45–60 minutes** with pan juices or melted butter/herb mixture (if the recipe calls for it). - **Butter basting**: Melt butter with herbs, spoon over turkey periodically. - **Cooking time**: - **Unbrined turkey**: ~13–15 minutes per pound (e.g., 12 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Brined turkey**: ~10–12 minutes per pound (e.g., 10 lbs = ~2 hours). - **Estimated total time**: 3–4 hours (including rest time). - **Thermometer check**: - Insert a **meat thermometer** into the thickest part of the thigh (avoid bone). - **Safe temp**: **165°F (74°C)** in the thickest part of the thigh and breast. - **Don’t overcook**: Turkeys continue cooking while resting (see below). #### **D. Resting (Non-Negotiable!)** - **Why**: Letting the turkey rest redistributes juices for moist meat. - **How**: - Tent loosely with foil and let rest **30–45 minutes** before carving. - Keep warm in the oven (turn off heat) or on a warming tray. --- ### **4. Carving and Serving** - **Carve at the table**: Use a sharp knife to slice against the grain. - **Serve with pan juices**: Strain and reduce juices for gravy if your recipe includes it. - **Leftovers**: Store in airtight containers (e.g., turkey, stuffing, gravy) within 2 hours of cooking. --- ### **5. Troubleshooting Common Issues** | **Problem** | **Solution** | |---------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | Turkey dries out | Brine it, baste often, or use a meat thermometer. | | Skin doesn’t brown | Broil for 2–3 minutes at the end (watch closely!). | | Stuffing gets soggy | Bake stuffing separately or stuff loosely. | | Overcooked | Remove from oven at 155°F (thigh) and rest. | | Turkey too salty | Rinse before cooking if brining; use unsalted butter. | --- ### **6. Pro Tips for First-Timers** - **Delegate**: Ask a family member to help with basting or carving. - **Set reminders**: Use phone alarms for basting intervals and thermometer checks. - **Document**: Take photos of each step to compare with the recipe later. - **Stay calm**: If something goes wrong (e.g., oven temp fluctuates), focus on the thermometer, not the clock. --- ### **7. Family-Specific Adjustments** If your family’s recipe includes unique elements (e.g.,: - **Herb butter**: Melt butter with herbs and rub under the skin. - **Apple cider brine**: Use apple cider instead of water for a subtle sweetness. - **Dry-brine**: Salt the turkey 1–2 days before cooking (no liquid brine). - **Herb stuffing**: Use a mix of celery, onions, breadcrumbs, and herbs. ), double-check these details with a family member. --- ### **8. Timeline Example (For a 12-lb Turkey)** | **Day Before** | **Morning Of** | **Cooking Day** | |--------------------------|-------------------------------|-------------------------------------| | Brine turkey (if needed) | Thaw turkey (if frozen) | Preheat oven to 325°F. | | Prep stuffing | Dry turkey, season | Place turkey in oven. | | | | Baste every 45 mins. | | | | Check temp at ~1.5 hours (155°F). | | | | Rest 30–45 mins before carving. | --- ### **Final Encouragement** You’ve got this! The key is to **follow the recipe closely**, **use a thermometer**, and **let the turkey rest**. Even if it’s not perfect, the love and effort will shine through. If you’re unsure about any step, don’t hesitate to ask for help—family traditions are meant to be shared. prediction.raw: This is a nuanced and emotionally complex scenario, and your feelings are entirely valid. Here’s my perspective on whether you acted appropriately (AITA) and why: ### **Why It’s Okay to Say No (AITA = Yes, but with nuance)** 1. **You Have No Meaningful Connection to the Deceased** - You’ve only met this great aunt once when you were an infant, and she’s never been mentioned in your life. This isn’t a case of avoiding a family member you’ve known but don’t particularly like—it’s more like being asked to attend a stranger’s funeral under the guise of family obligation. - **Respect is reciprocal**: If you don’t know the person or their role in the family, attending out of obligation feels hollow. True respect comes from genuine connection, not performative attendance. 2. **You’re Not Asked to Attend for Yourself—Just for Your Mum** - Your mum’s motivation seems to be about *her* grief and *her* need for support (e.g., seeing extended family), not about honoring your great aunt. This is a subtle but important distinction. - If she wanted you there for *your* reasons (e.g., "We should support each other through this"), that might feel different. But when the expectation is tied to *her* needs rather than yours or the deceased’s, it’s harder to justify. 3. **Funerals Are Emotionally Taxing for You** - You’ve acknowledged that you’re awkward at funerals, especially for people you barely know. That’s a valid reason to decline—you’re not being disrespectful; you’re being honest about your capacity. - Forcing yourself into such settings can lead to discomfort, guilt, or even resentment. It’s okay to prioritize your emotional well-being. 4. **The Guilt-Tripping Is Unfair** - Your mum’s reaction ("Fine, I’ll go on my own") suggests she’s using emotional leverage (e.g., "I’ll handle it alone if you don’t care"). This isn’t a healthy way to encourage attendance. If she truly wanted you there, she’d frame it as a shared experience, not a demand. - **Healthy family dynamics** involve mutual respect. If she can’t accept your boundaries, that’s a red flag about how she handles grief or expectations. --- ### **Why Some Might Argue Otherwise (AITA = No, but with caveats)** 1. **"It’s Family—You Should Be There"** - Some cultures or families place a heavy emphasis on attendance at funerals as a duty, regardless of personal connection. If this is your family’s norm, you might feel pressure to conform. - **Counterpoint**: If the expectation is purely traditional (not tied to your mum’s grief or the deceased’s legacy), it’s worth questioning whether this is truly about respect or obligation. 2. **"You’ll Miss Out on Seeing Extended Family"** - Your mum highlights that this is one of the few times you’ll see this branch of the family. While this is true, it doesn’t mean you *have* to attend the funeral itself. You could suggest alternatives: - Attending a separate family gathering (e.g., a meal or reunion) after the funeral. - Offering to help your mum in other ways (e.g., driving her, helping with logistics) to show support without being present at the service. 3. **"You Might Regret Not Going Later"** - Some people worry about "what if" scenarios (e.g., "What if I never get another chance to see them?"). This is a natural fear, but it’s not a reason to force yourself into an uncomfortable situation. - **Reality check**: You *will* see this family again. Life is unpredictable, but funerals aren’t the only way to connect. Your mum’s argument here feels more about her needs than yours. --- ### **What You Could Do Instead** If you want to honor your mum’s feelings while respecting your own boundaries, try these approaches: 1. **Frame It as a Shared Experience (Without Forcing Attendance)** - *"I know this is hard for you, Mum. I can’t go to the funeral, but I’ll be there for you afterward—whether that’s helping with the meal, driving you, or just sitting with you. You don’t have to go alone."* - This validates her grief while setting a boundary. 2. **Suggest an Alternative** - *"I’d love to see the family, but I’m not comfortable at funerals. Can we plan a separate time to get together?"* - This shows you’re willing to engage without compromising your comfort. 3. **Address the Guilt-Tripping Directly** - If she continues to guilt you, you can say: *"I’m not avoiding this because I don’t care. I just don’t feel like I can be there for someone I barely knew. But I’m here for you."* - This shifts the focus from obligation to support. 4. **Reflect on the Underlying Issue** - Why is this great aunt’s death being brought up *now*? Why hasn’t she been mentioned before? This might reveal deeper family dynamics (e.g., unresolved grief, generational trauma, or your mum’s way of processing loss). If you’re curious, you could gently ask: *"Mum, I’ve never heard of Great Aunt Wyn before today. Was she important to you? I’d love to understand why this feels so meaningful now."* --- ### **Final Verdict: You’re Not Wrong** Your feelings are **completely valid**. You’re not being disrespectful—you’re being honest about your limits. Funerals are deeply personal, and attending one for someone you don’t know isn’t a duty; it’s an expectation that may not align with your emotional capacity. That said, the *how* you communicate this matters. Instead of a passive "no" (which can feel dismissive), try the suggestions above to show empathy while standing your ground. Your mum’s reaction ("I’ll go alone") suggests she might not be handling this well, which is sad but not your responsibility to fix. **Score: 1 (You acted appropriately)** You’re not obligated to attend a funeral for someone you don’t know, especially when the expectation feels tied to your mum’s needs rather than yours or the deceased’s. The key is to communicate your boundaries with kindness and clarity.
